Total Synthesis Hot Paper
Total Syntheses of (/C0)-Conidiogenone B, (/C0)-Conidiogenone, and (/C0)-
Conidiogenol
Bo Xu+, Wen Xun +, Shaobin Su, and Hongbin Zhai*
In memory of Professor Jack E. Baldwin
Abstract: Cyclopianes are novel diterpenes featuring a highly
strained 6/5/5/5 tetracyclic core embedded with 6–8 consecutive
stereocenters. The concise total syntheses of ( /C0)-conidiogeno-
ne B, ( /C0)-conidiogenone, and ( /C0)-conidiogenol have been
accomplished in 14–17 steps. The present work features a HAT -
mediated alkene–nitrile cyclization to access the cis-biquinane,
a Nicholas/Pauson–Khand reaction to construct the linear
triquinane, and a Danheiser annulation to afford the congested
angular triquinane skeleton.
Cyclopianes are novel diterpenes featuring a highly strained
6/5/5/5 tetracyclic core embedded with 6–8 consecutive
stereocenters, four of which are quaternary carbon centers
(Figure 1). The structural variations of cyclopianes are mainly
manifested as differences in the oxidation state of certain
carbon atoms within the skeleton. Since the first isolation of
conidiogenone ( 1) and conidiogenol ( 2) by Sterner and co-
workers in 2002, more than 20 compounds of this family have
been isolated from the genus Penicillium.
[1] Interestingly,
cyclopiane diterpenes display a range of biological activities.
Conidiogenone ( 1) and conidiogenol ( 2) as inducers of
conidiogenesis in P . cyclopium may become new tool
compounds for the study of the morphogenetic event. [1a]
Conidiogenone B ( 3) shows significant antibacterial activity
against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA;
MIC = 8 mgm L/C01).[1d] Conidiogenone C ( 4) exhibits potent
cytotoxicity against HL60 cells (IC 50 = 38 nm).[1c]
The structural complexity and the significant biological
activities of cyclopianes have aroused broad interest from the
synthetic community.
[2] In 2016, T u and co-workers accom-
plished the first total syntheses of cyclopiane diterpenoids,
featuring a one-step regioselective and diastereoselective
semipinacol-type rearrangement strategy.
[2a] In 2019, Snyder
and co-workers reported the asymmetric total syntheses of
cyclopiane diterpenoids guided by quaternary center analy-
sis.
[2b] In addition to the chemical synthesis, the biosynthetic
pathway of conidiogenone was fully elucidated through
heterologous expression of biosynthetic genes in Aspergillus
oryzae and by in vitro enzyme assay with
13C-labeled sub-
strates in 2019. [3]
The synthesis of angular triquinane natural products has
continued to be an active research area in organic chemistry.
In the past decades, many novel synthetic strategies for
angular triquinane skeleton natural products have been
developed.
[4] Inspired by Schmidt and Knçlker/C29s work, [5]
which utilized a Lewis acid mediated allylsilane [3 +2] cyclo-
addition strategy to forge the angular triquinane skeleton, we
became fascinated with the development of a general Danhe-
iser annulation strategy toward the construction of angular
triquinane natural products including silphinene ( 7), retiger-
anic acid A ( 8), and crinipellin A ( 9; Figure 2 A). Danheiser
annulation of allenylsilanes with electron-deficient olefins is
a powerful and straightforward method for the synthesis of
highly substituted cyclopentenes.
[6] However, this annulation
has received little attention from synthetic organic chemists
since its first publication by Danheiser in 1981. In particular, it
has not been extensively examined for the synthesis of
complex natural products.
[7] Herein, we report the total
syntheses of ( /C0)-conidiogenone B, ( /C0)-conidiogenone, and
(/C0)-conidiogenol featuring a Danheiser annulation reaction
for the rapid assembly of the challenging tetracyclic skeleton
of these natural products.

ne B (3) could be constructed through an aldol approach from
keto aldehyde 13, which could be obtained by ozonolysis of
the trisubstituted olefin 14. The congested angular triquinane
portion of the tetraquinane 14 could be accessed efficiently
through a [3 +2] Danheiser annulation, and the key linear
triquinane 16 could be readily derived via a tandem Nicholas/
Pauson–Khand reaction sequence from 17, which in turn
could be traced back to trimethylcyclopentenone 18.[8]
As outlined in Scheme 1, our synthesis commenced with
the Corey–Bakshi–Shibata reduction [9] of the readily avail-
able trimethylcyclopentenone 18,[8] providing the correspond-
ing allylic alcohol 19 in 90 % yield with 92 % ee (as
determined by the HPLC analysis of the corresponding p-
nitrobenzoate). T reatment of allylic alcohol 19 with n-butyl
vinyl ether in the presence of Hg(OAc) 2 and Et 3N at 170 8C
completed a tandem vinylation/Claisen rearrangement reac-
tion sequence
[10] to afford the desired aldehyde, one-carbon
homologation of which through van Leusen reaction [11]
furnished nitrile 20 in 71 % yield. The iron-mediated HAT
alkene–nitrile cyclization of 20 under Talbot/C29s conditions
provided bicyclic ketone 21 (74 %).[12] Examination of several
conventional methods (such as TMSOTf/ m-CPBA, LDA/
Davis oxaziridine, LDA/MoOPH) for achieving the a-
hydroxylation ketone 22 proved problematic. Fortunately,
MeReO3-catalyzed Rubottom oxidation was effective for this
transformation and the reaction led reproducibly to the
desired product 22 in high yield (91 %, /C2110:1 d.r.). [13]
Addition of 1-propynyl Grignard to 22 afforded the vicinal
diol 23 in 76 % yield, oxidative cleavage of which by using
Pb(OAc)4 followed by direct reduction of both carbonyl
groups under Luche conditions generated 24 in 80 % yield.
Chemoselective transformation of the primary hydroxy group
in 24 to give 17 (82 %) through Grieco/C29s method
[14] set the
stage for the key Nicholas/Pauson–Khand reaction sequence.
Even though the combination of Nicholas and Pauson–Khand
reactions into a one-pot fashion would enable synthetic
efficiency enhancement, the sole application of this strategy
that had been reported was Schreiber/C29s synthesis of epox-
ydictymene.
[15] Gratifyingly, enyne alcohol 17 was subjected to
a Nicholas reaction with borane-methyl sulfide complex as
the hydride source, [16] followed by amine-N-oxide-promoted
Pauson–Khand reaction,[17] to furnish triquinane 16 as a single
diastereomer in 71 % yield. To the best of our knowledge, this
represents the first example of tandem Nicholas/Pauson–
Khand reactions involving a hydride reduction step.
We next turned our attention to the key Danheiser
annulation to forge a five-membered ring with concomitant
establishment of two all-carbon quaternary carbon centers.
T reatment of 16 and commercial allene 15 a with TiCl
4 at
/C078 8C afforded the desired tetraquinane 28 a bearing two
quaternary carbons in 91 % yield. Encouraged by this result,
we envisioned that allene 15 b would also be effective for the
reaction. Indeed, the cyclization did take place to generate
tetraquinane 28 b in 33 % yield along with the competing
Hosomi–Sakurai product 29 b in 46 % yield. The Sakurai-type
product presumably resulted from insufficient stability of the
intermediary vinyl cation. We speculated that increasing the
bulkiness of the silyl group in the allenylsilane might prevent
the formation of the Sakurai-type byproduct. Thus, a bulky
TIPS group was employed to replace TMS for allene 15 c, and
in this case the desired 28 c was obtained in a much better
yield (89 %), together with less than 5 % of the Sakurai-type
byproduct 29 c. Subsequent one-pot desilylation of 28 c with
a boron trifluoride acetic acid complex provided the desired
tetraquinane 25 in 89 % yield (d.r. > 4:1). The relative
stereochemistry of 25 was established through 2D NMR
spectroscopy and further corroborated by X-ray analysis of
the corresponding tosylhydrazone ent-30. It is reasonable to
assume that the transition state conformation TS-B was more
favored over TS-A as shown in Figure 3. At this point, the
carbonyl had to be fully reduced to methylene. Wolff–
Kishner–Huang-Minlon reduction
[18] of ketone 25 was prob-
lematic since the desired full reduction product 14 was
obtained in only 37 % yield. Modified Wolff–Kishner reduc-
tion of tosylhydrazone 30 also proved to be ineffective with
a variety of different reducing agents such as NaBH
3CN,
catecholborane, LiAlH4, or Dibal-H.[19] Nevertheless, a three-
step Barton–McCombie deoxygenation approach successfully
afforded tetracycle 14 in 51 % overall yield. [20]
With the requisite angular triquinane framework in hand,
we began to investigate the ring-enlargement process. Ozo-
nolysis of the trisubstituted carbon-carbon double bond in
tetraquinane 14 provided keto aldehyde 13, which was
directly used for the subsequent aldol reaction. Prior to the
planned aldol condensation for the generation of ( /C0)-
conidiogenone B ( 3), we first examined the feasibility of
direct conversion of keto-aldehyde 13 into (/C0)-conidiogenone
(1) through a stereoselective aldol reaction. However, the

attempts (Table 1). Surprisingly, treatment of aldehyde 13
with p-toluenesulfonic acid in dry toluene at 80 8C afforded

It is worth noting that the concentration of aqueous HCl was
critical to avoiding the formation of the undesired product 31.
Isomerization of 26 to (/C0)-conidiogenone B ( 3) was achieved
by treatment with RhCl
3 (Keq /C250.5). Finally, stereoselective
epoxidation[2a] of ( /C0)-conidiogenone B with TBHP followed
by reduction of the resultant epoxide with SmI 2
[21] furnished
(/C0)-conidiogenone ( 1). Reduction of ( /C0)-conidiogenone ( 1)
with L-selectride delivered ( /C0)-conidiogenol ( 2)i n8 4 %
yield. The spectroscopic data of the synthetic sample match
those reported.

In summary, a concise total synthesis of ( /C0)-conidioge-
none B has been achieved in 14 steps and with 4.7 % overall
yield from readily available trimethylcyclopentenone 18.[8]
Moreover, ( /C0)-conidiogenone and ( /C0)-conidiogenol were
also realized through a modified T u protocol.[2a] The synthesis
features a HAT-mediated alkene–nitrile cyclization to access
the cis-biquinane, a sequential Nicholas/Pauson–Khand reac-
tions for the construction of the linear triquinane, a Danheiser
annulation to forge the congested angular triquinane portion,
and a combined ozonolysis/aldol reaction to assemble the a,b-
unsaturated cyclohexenone skeleton. The current work may
facilitate larger-scale preparation and further biological
studies of various cyclopiane natural products.
